subject: Science
theme: Nuclear fusion technology and ITER's immediate strategic advantage for India
question_short_text: What is India's immediate advantage from ITER success?
text: India is an important member of the 'International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor'. If this experiment succeeds, what is the immediate advantage for India?
options: It can use thorium in place of uranium for power generation
It can attain a global role in satellite navigation
It can drastically improve the efficiency of its fission reactors in power generation
It can build fusion reactors for power generation
answerText: (d) It can build fusion reactors for power generation
explanation: ITER's success would demonstrate fusion technology feasibility and provide India with the scientific knowledge, technical capabilities, and intellectual property access needed to develop domestic fusion reactors for clean energy production.

research.summary: ITER is fundamentally a scientific and technology demonstration project, not a commercial power plant. Its core mission is to prove that fusion can achieve net energy gain (Q ≥ 10) and to test all the integrated technologies required for a future fusion power plant. The key trap in this question lies in understanding what 'immediate advantage' actually means in this context. Option (c) about improving fission reactor efficiency is incorrect because ITER deals with fusion, which is an entirely different process from fission and has no direct bearing on existing fission reactor design. Option (a) about thorium use is also incorrect; ITER involves deuterium-tritium fusion, not thorium fuel cycles. Option (b) about satellite navigation is unrelated and serves as a distractor. The correct answer is (d) because, under the ITER Agreement, all member nations—including India, which contributes 9% of construction costs—gain access to 100% of the intellectual property and experimental results. This means India would directly acquire the scientific knowledge, engineering expertise, and technological blueprints needed to design, build, and operate its own fusion demonstration reactor (DEMO) in the future. ITER itself will not generate electricity for the grid; instead, it serves as the experimental bridge between today's small fusion research machines and tomorrow's commercial power plants. India has already demonstrated commitment to this path: it operates the ADITYA and SST-1 tokamaks domestically, and it is a skilled contributor to ITER, having fabricated the massive 30-metre cryostat and other critical systems. Success of ITER would validate fusion as a viable energy source and position India to transition from a research phase to reactor development and ultimately to commercial fusion power generation within the second half of this century.
facts: India contributes 9% of ITER construction costs and receives 100% access to intellectual property and experimental results, a substantial strategic advantage.

ITER is designed to achieve a fusion gain (Q) of 10—meaning 500 MW of fusion thermal power output from 50 MW of input heating power—for the first time in history, proving the technical feasibility of fusion at scale.

India's domestic fusion program includes ADITYA (operational since 1989) and SST-1 tokamaks, which have built the engineering and physics expertise necessary to be a major ITER partner and to eventually design a domestic demonstration (DEMO) reactor.
